Appendix A Probes of the Quantum Kibble-Zurek (QKZ) Mechanism

In this supplementary section, we discuss physical aspects related to the two annealing protocols considered in Sec. IV.1.

According to the QKZ mechanism, during an annealing sweep across a continuous quantum critical point, the rapid divergence of the ground-state correlation length in the vicinity of the transition point can no longer be followed once non-adiabatic effects become significant. Instead, the system “freezes out” over a characteristic time scale t^\hat{t} and length scale η^\hat{\eta}, leading to universal scaling laws for excitations and correlations. The QKZ mechanism has been explored in one-dimensional systems [113, 38], but quantitative tests in two-dimensional interacting quantum matter remain comparatively scarce. Recent work by Schmitt et. al. in Ref. [78] provides a numerical analysis of QKZ scaling in 2D, establishing clear data collapse of correlation functions and excitation energies under appropriate rescaling according to the non-equilibrium scaling hypothesis.

In our study, we investigate the 2D Ising model on a square lattice under two distinct annealing protocols, Annealing (I) and Annealing (II), in this section we probe whether the QKZ mechanism governs the resulting dynamics. To do so, we replicate the scaling analysis performed in Ref. [78] by computing the equal-time spin–spin correlation function close to the critical point during the annealing schedule and rescaling both the correlation distance and correlation amplitude using the theoretically predicted QKZ freeze-out scales. This procedure provides a direct diagnostic of universal KZ behavior: if the annealing schedule places the system within the QKZ regime; meaning the freeze-out length η^\hat{\eta} remains well below the system size, the rescaled correlation functions obtained at various quench rates must collapse onto a single universal curve.

Our results in Fig. 11 show a sharp distinction between the two annealing schedules. Under Annealing (I), the rescaled correlation functions fail to collapse, indicating that, due to the finite-size gap in the vicinity of the crossing point, non-adiabatic effects do not play a fundamental role and that the dynamics is in the quasi-adiabatic regime. In contrast, Annealing (II) produces a robust collapse of the rescaled correlations across a wide range of annealing times. This behavior mirrors the finite-size scaling results reported in Ref. [78] and demonstrates that Annealing (II) traverses the near-critical region at rates that generate universal excitations where η^/L≪1\hat{\eta}/L\ll 1. This findings confirm that only Annealing (II) probes the QKZ regime in our simulations.

Note, in Fig. 11 we use the theoretically predicted values for rescaling, i.e. ξ^∝τν/(1+z​ν)\hat{\xi}\propto\tau^{\nu/(1+z\nu)} and 2​Δ=1+η2\Delta=1+\eta with z=1z=1, ν=0.629971\nu=0.629971 and η=0.036298​(2)\eta=0.036298(2). In the work of Schmitt et. al. it was found that finite size effects lead to a slight deviation from these values - it is likely that an even stronger collapse could observed in the results of this work with similar considerations.

Appendix B Additional results

B.1 Further tests of the Symmetry Convergence Criterion

In this supplementary section, we provide additional details on the implementation of the symmetry-based convergence criterion introduced in the main text. Our goal is to show how this criterion can be used to regularize numerical results and identify regions of trustworthy dynamics. We focus primarily on MPS, as it is the most widely used method in the literature, examine results with systematically increasing bond dimensions, results obtained from different MPS mappings, and investigate the effect of increasing system size on the timescales over which the dynamics remain converged according to our criterion. Finally, we compare the “converged” results from MPS and TTN with those obtained from benchmark methods, including 2DTN and NQS, to assess the reliability and limitations of the different tensor-network approaches.

In Fig. 12 we show the symmetry errors and corresponding dynamics for both local observables, panels (a1–a2), and connected correlation, panels (b1–b2) as a function of time for increasing MPS bond dimension. As expected, lower bond dimensions lead to earlier growth of asymmetries, indicating a breakdown of the approximate wave function. The convergence criterion effectively identifies the portions of the dynamics where the results begin to deviate as the bond dimension is increased, marking the boundary of the reliably converged regime. Interestingly, the criterion also reveals that connected correlations start to deviate from one another earlier than local observables, highlighting that long-range quantities are more sensitive to the limitations of the MPS representation.

In Fig. 13 we compare results obtained from two different MPS mappings of the 10×1010\times 10 square lattice: a horizontal snaking pattern (black) and a diagonal snaking pattern (green). Panel (a) illustrates the two mappings, while panel (b) shows the corresponding symmetry errors for both local magnetization and connected correlations following a quench to hx/J=2.0h_{x}/J=2.0. Panels (c) and (d) display the time evolution of these observables, with dotted points indicating regions where the results are no longer considered converged according to the symmetry-based criterion.

It is well known that the choice of MPS mapping plays a critical role in accurately capturing long-range correlations. Optimal mappings are typically chosen to preserve locality: nodes that are connected in the MPS should correspond to physically nearby sites on the lattice. Different mapping choices can therefore lead to quantitatively different results, particularly for observables sensitive to long-range correlations. It is also interesting to note that different mappings will break or preserve different symmetries from the D4D_{4} subgroup, which could further influence the growth of symmetry errors and the apparent convergence of the simulation.

This sensitivity provides a natural test for the convergence criterion. By comparing results obtained from different mappings, we can assess whether the criterion reliably identifies portions of the dynamics where the approximate MPS wave function ceases to be accurate. As shown in panels (c) and (d) of Fig. 13, for both local magnetization and connected correlations, the divergence between the two mappings coincides with the symmetry-error criterion flagging the results as unconverged. This demonstrates that the convergence criterion effectively captures the breakdown of the approximation and identifies the time windows over which the dynamics can be trusted.

In Fig. 14 we show the bond dimension required to achieve convergence for both local magnetization (panel a) and connected correlations (panel b) as a function of system size and simulation time. For short-time dynamics, a relatively small bond dimension is sufficient, as the amount of entanglement generated during these early times remains modest. However, as the simulation progresses to longer times, the required bond dimension increases to accurately capture the growing entanglement. Similarly, larger system sizes demand higher bond dimensions for the same simulation time, reflecting the known result that capturing long-range correlations in extended systems becomes increasingly difficult. Notably, we see directly that, to converge to the same time and system size, connected correlations require higher bond dimensions than local magnetization, highlighting their greater sensitivity to the limitations of the MPS representation.

B.2 Full annealing results

In Figs. 15 and 16 we present the full set of annealing results analyzed in this work for all system sizes studied. Figure 15 shows the time evolution of the local magnetization, ⟨σr0z⟩\langle\sigma_{r_{0}}^{z}\rangle, for annealing sweeps (I) and (II) (corresponding to panels a1 and b1 in Fig. 4 of the main text), while Fig. 16 displays the nearest-neighbor connected correlations, C⁡(δ1)C(\delta_{1}), for the same sweeps (corresponding to panels a1 and b1 in Fig. 5). Results are obtained with MPS, TTN, NQS, and 2DTN.

As the annealing protocol is also defined on a square lattice and the Hamiltonian respects the D4D_{4} symmetry, the same symmetry-based convergence criterion used for the quench dynamics can be applied here. Deviations in the local observables and connected correlations along symmetry-equivalent sites indicate the onset of unphysical asymmetries, allowing us to identify the time windows where MPS and TTN simulations remain reliable. Thus, vertical lines indicate the times up to which MPS and TTN results are considered converged according to the symmetry-based convergence criterion.

These figures demonstrate that the convergence criterion successfully identifies the times at which MPS and TTN begin to deviate from each other as well as from other methods in most cases, providing a reliable measure of the time window over which each method produces trustworthy dynamics. Across all system sizes, the criterion captures both early-time agreement and the onset of deviations in long-time dynamics, validating its effectiveness as a practical tool for benchmarking tensor-network simulations.

B.3 Full post-quench dynamics results

In Figs. 17 and 18 we present the full set of post-quench dynamics results analyzed in this work for all system sizes studied. Figure 17 shows the time evolution of the local magnetization, ⟨σr0z⟩\langle\sigma_{r_{0}}^{z}\rangle, for quench strengths hx/J=0.5h_{x}/J=0.5, 2.02.0, and 3.03.0 (corresponding to panels a1, b1, and c1 in Fig. 6 of the main text). Figure 18 displays the nearest-neighbor connected correlations, C⁡(δ1)C(\delta_{1}), for the same quench strengths (corresponding to panels a1, b1, and c1 in Fig. 7 of the main text). Results are obtained with MPS, TTN, NQS, and 2DTN. Vertical lines indicate the times up to which MPS and TTN results are considered converged according to the symmetry-based convergence criterion.

These figures demonstrate that the convergence criterion reliably identifies the times at which MPS and TTN begin to deviate from each other as well as from other numerical methods in most cases. Across all system sizes and quench strengths, the criterion captures both early-time agreement and the onset of deviations in long-time dynamics, validating its effectiveness as a practical tool for benchmarking tensor-network simulations of quench dynamics.

Appendix C TDVP error for tree tensor networks

In this section we provide a derivation for the TDVP error (15) used for quantifying the accuracy of the TTN simulations. Starting from eq. (13), we rewrite the evolved variational state using the tangent-space projector P^\hat{P}

|ψθ→​(t+δ​t)⟩=e−i​P^​H^​δ​t​|ψθ→​(t)⟩,\ket{\psi_{\vec{\theta}(t+\delta t)}}=e^{-i\hat{P}\hat{H}\delta t}\ket{\psi_{\vec{\theta}(t)}}\ , (21)

which is the form typically used in formulations of the TDVP equation for tensor network states. Following the derivation from [76], consisting of an expansion of the exponential up to second order in δ​t\delta t, and identifying ℰ=−i​H^​δ​t\mathcal{E}=-i\hat{H}\delta t and R=−i​P^​H^​δ​tR=-i\hat{P}\hat{H}\delta t, we arrive at eq. (15) from the main text.

Note, that the quantities appearing in the equation can be calculated efficiently using the already existing, effective environments of the TDVP algorithm.

Appendix D Neural quantum states

In this Section, we describe some important details of the NQS-tVMC simulations considered in this work.

We parametrize the wave function ψθ→​(s)\psi_{\vec{\theta}}(s), where θ→\vec{\theta} is a set of variational parameters parametrised by NQS architectures, which consist of a two-layer Convolutional Neural Networks with α\alpha and α−1\alpha-1 channels in the two consecutive layers. The equation of motion of such variational parameters is given by

Sk,k′​θ˙k′=−i​Fk,S_{k,k^{\prime}}\dot{\theta}_{k^{\prime}}=-iF_{k}\ , (22)

where θ˙k′\dot{\theta}_{k^{\prime}} is the time derivative,

Sk,k′=⟨∂θkψθ→|∂θk′ψθ→⟩−⟨∂θkψθ→|ψθ→⟩​⟨ψθ→|∂θk′ψθ→⟩\begin{split}S_{k,k^{\prime}}=\braket{\partial_{\theta_{k}}\psi_{\vec{\theta}}|\partial_{\theta_{k^{\prime}}}\psi_{\vec{\theta}}}-\braket{\partial_{\theta_{k}}\psi_{\vec{\theta}}|\psi_{\vec{\theta}}}\braket{\psi_{\vec{\theta}}|\partial_{\theta_{k^{\prime}}}\psi_{\vec{\theta}}}\end{split} (23)

is the quantum Fisher matrix and

Fk=⟨∂θkψθ→|H^|ψθ→⟩−⟨∂θkψθ→|ψθ→⟩​⟨ψθ→|H^|ψθ→⟩.\begin{split}F_{k}=\braket{\partial_{\theta_{k}}\psi_{\vec{\theta}}|\hat{H}|\psi_{\vec{\theta}}}-\braket{\partial_{\theta_{k}}\psi_{\vec{\theta}}|\psi_{\vec{\theta}}}\braket{\psi_{\vec{\theta}}|\hat{H}|\psi_{\vec{\theta}}}.\end{split} (24)

Both Sk,k′S_{k,k^{\prime}} and FkF_{k} can be estimated via Monte-Carlo sampling of the Born distribution |ψθ→​(s)|2|\psi_{\vec{\theta}}(s)|^{2}.

The time evolution of the variational parameters θ\theta is performed by numerically solving Eq. 22 with the second-order Heun method with a fixed time interval of δt​J=10−2\delta_{t}J=10^{-2}.

Furthermore, an important technical detail is that the SS matrix turns out to be ill-conditioned (i.e., it can contain an eigenvalue spectrum that spans all numerical orders of magnitude). Therefore, the time evolution via tVMC requires suitable regularization schemes when inverting the SS matrix to solve Eq.(22). In particular, we consider the scheme proposed in ref. [76], which is based on a targeted elimination of noisy contributions of singular values of SS.

D.0.1 NQS-tVMC simulations with different local basis

A second important detail is that the simulations of the dynamics of the initial-time product state in the computational basis (as in Eq.2) pose issues for tVMC simulations. First, simply because the SS-matrix vanishes for such a state. Second, the variational states whose probability distribution (|ψθ→​(s)|2|\psi_{\vec{\theta}}(s)|^{2}) is equal to zero for many basis states, but yield finite contributions to the gradients, is know to bias estimators of certain observables (e.g., as the ones necessary to access FF), which can demand an exponentially large number of samples [91].

To circumvent such issues, we consider simulations performed in a rotated basis. In order to implement such basis rotations in our simulations, we consider a unitary transformation of the Hamiltonian, H~​(γ)=U^​(γ)​H​U^†​(γ)\tilde{H}(\gamma)=\hat{U}(\gamma)\,H\,\hat{U}^{\dagger}(\gamma), where γ\gamma is the parameter of the unitary transformation. Particularly, in this work, we consider simulations to a more specific choice of local basis defined by the unitary transformation:

U^(γ)=∏k=1Ne−iσkyγk/2,\hat{U}(\gamma)=\prod_{k=1}^{N}e^{-i\sigma_{k}^{y}\gamma_{k}/2}, (25)

we consider a uniform γk=γ\gamma_{k}=\gamma.

The time dependence of an observable AA can then be written as

⟨ψ⁡(0)|​ei​H​t​A^​e−i​H​t​|ψ⁡(0)⟩=⟨ψ~​(0)|​ei​H~​t​(U^​A^​U^†)​e−i​H~​t​|ψ~​(0)⟩.\begin{split}\bra{\psi(0)}e^{iHt}\hat{A}e^{-iHt}\ket{\psi(0)}=\\ \bra{\tilde{\psi}(0)}e^{i\tilde{H}t}(\hat{U}\hat{A}\hat{U}^{\dagger})e^{-i\tilde{H}t}\ket{\tilde{\psi}(0)}.\end{split} (26)

Our strategy is therefore as follows: instead of simulating the dynamics generated by the original Hamiltonian HH, we simulate the dynamics of the transformed Hamiltonian H~\tilde{H}, with the initial state |ψ~​(0)⟩{\ket{\tilde{\psi}(0)}} being the ground state of Hamiltonian H~​(γ)\tilde{H}(\gamma) with hx=0h_{x}=0.

For all the results presented in Sec. II.1 for the quantum annealing protocols we consider γπ=0.1\frac{\gamma}{\pi}=0.1, while in Sec. II.2 for the post-quench dynamics we consider γπ=0.1\frac{\gamma}{\pi}=0.1 for hx/J=2.0h_{x}/J=2.0 and γπ=0.3\frac{\gamma}{\pi}=0.3 for hx/J=0.3h_{x}/J=0.3.

Appendix E Two-dimensional tensor networks with belief propagation

In this section, we discuss the effect of changing the bond dimension used in the 2DTN-BP method. In Fig. 19, we illustrate the behavior for the particular case of post-quench dynamics at hx/J=2.0h_{x}/J=2.0 and L=10L=10, for which we show the difference in the truncation error for χ2​D=40\chi_{2D}=40 (used to obtain the results of the main text) and a lower χ2​D=32\chi_{2D}=32. In terms of peak RAM during these Trotter evolutions, the simulation at χ2​D=32\chi_{2D}=32 used ≈12\approx 12 GB, while the one with χ2​D=40\chi_{2D}=40 used ≈24\approx 24 GB. Despite this increase in the computational resources, we observe that increasing the bond dimension only slightly shifts the time at which the truncation errors starts to grow exponentially.

Appendix F Simulation Runtimes

In this section, we summarize the computational runtimes for the numerical methods used in this work. The simulations were performed for two annealing schedules, Anneal (I) and Anneal (II), followed by post-quench dynamics with hx/J=2.0h_{x}/J=2.0. The runtimes reported here correspond to the average time required to complete a single time-step for a given simulation, including all stages of the calculation, see Table. 1.

In the MPS simulations performed, the bond dimension was dynamically adjusted to saturate the full 40 GB memory capacity of an NVIDIA A100 GPU. Because the maximum feasible bond dimension decreases with increasing system size, this leads to system-size–dependent truncation thresholds. For instance, when simulating a system of size L=8L=8, the GPU memory allowed us to reach a bond dimension of 1600. In contrast, for L=14L=14 the same memory constraint limited the bond dimension to 700. As a result, the runtime cannot be meaningfully compared across system sizes, since each simulation effectively uses a different truncation regime.

Appendix G Mean-field and semiclassical solutions

While the main part of this work focused on strongly correlated methods, these methods quickly become inefficient in describing large system sizes in higher dimensions. For such systems, the pool of available numerical methods which can still be used to simulate the underlying spin dynamics while capturing some form of entanglement or correlation is much more limited. In light of rapid improvements in experimental control of quantum systems beyond 100 particles, one has to resort to computationally less demanding many-body methods that are able to deal with large system sizes. However, such computational methods are often restricted to families of quantum states which can only capture a limited amount of entanglement and typically only work well on short time scales.

In the following, we consider three methods that can be applied to study the dynamics of large spin-1/2 systems: We will consider (i) a spin mean-field (SMF) theory, (ii) a fermionic mean-field theory based on parity-violating fermionic Gaussian states (PV-FGS), and (iii) a method based on the discrete truncated Wigner approximation (TW). While (i) can be considered as a purely classical mean-field solution incapable of capturing correlations or entanglement, (ii) adds quadratic corrections to its mean-field solution and is able to introduce entanglement in spin systems [68, 36]. Method (iii) describes a semiclassical theory which is able to accurately describe the short-time non-equilibrium dynamics of large spin systems [75].

Spin mean-field theory:

A system of non-interacting spins can be described by a spin-1/2 product state

|Ψ⟩=⨂j=1N(αj​|0⟩j+βj​|1⟩j),\displaystyle\ket{\Psi}=\bigotimes_{j=1}^{N}\left(\alpha_{j}\ket{0}_{j}+\beta_{j}\ket{1}_{j}\right), (27)

where αj∈ℝ\alpha_{j}\in\mathds{R} and βj∈ℂ\beta_{j}\in\mathds{C}, with |αj|2+|βj|2=1|\alpha_{j}|^{2}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}=1. The mean-field approximation is given by σiz​σjz≈σiz​⟨σjz⟩+⟨σiz⟩​σjz−⟨σiz⟩​⟨σjz⟩\sigma^{z}_{i}\sigma^{z}_{j}\approx\sigma^{z}_{i}\braket{\sigma^{z}_{j}}+\braket{\sigma^{z}_{i}}\sigma^{z}_{j}-\braket{\sigma^{z}_{i}}\braket{\sigma^{z}_{j}} which leads to en effective self-consistent mean-field potential [108]. This approximation works usually well if quadratic fluctuations around the mean value of the spin variables are small. Using a time-dependent variational principle, real-time equations of motion can be derived either for the variational wave function parameters αj\alpha_{j} and βj\beta_{j} [55], or, equivalently, for the spin observables directly [75].

Fermionic mean-field theory:

Similar to Eq. (27), we consider parity-violating fermionic Gaussian states (PV-FGS) [85]

|Ψ⟩=\displaystyle\ket{\Psi}= exp⁡(12​(𝐜†𝐜)​𝐌​(𝐜𝐜†)+𝐮†​𝐜†+𝐯T​𝐜)​|0⟩⊗N,\displaystyle\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{c}^{\dagger}&\mathbf{c}\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{c}\\ \mathbf{c}^{\dagger}\end{pmatrix}+\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{c}^{\dagger}+\mathbf{v}^{T}\mathbf{c}\right)\ket{0}^{\otimes N}, (28)

where 𝐜^=(c^1,c^2,…,c^N)T\hat{\mathbf{c}}=(\hat{c}_{1},\hat{c}_{2},\dots,\hat{c}_{N})^{T} is a vector of fermionic creation operators, 𝐌\mathbf{M} is a suitable matrix, 𝐮,𝐯\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v} are vectors, chosen so that the argument of the exponent is anti-Hermitian. While previous fermionic mean-field methods have focused on parity preserving FGS, i.e. states where uj=vj=0u_{j}=v_{j}=0 for all j∈[1,…​2​N]j\in[1,\dots 2N], which can be efficiently described using the method outlined in Ref. [90], studying a spin Hamiltonian that maps to a PV fermionic Hamiltonian, or quenches from an initial state which cannot be described by a parity-preserving FGS require the study of the more complex PV-FGS ansätze (28), where i.g. uj,vj≠0u_{j},v_{j}\neq 0. A comprehensive account of the method will be given in a forthcoming publication [37].

Discrete truncated Wigner approximation:

TW formulates spin dynamics in discrete phase space [75]. Expectation values are written as ⟨O^​(t)⟩=∑αwα​OαW​(t),\braket{\hat{O}(t)}=\sum_{\alpha}w_{\alpha}\,O^{W}_{\alpha}(t), where α\alpha indexes the 4N4^{N} phase points, wαw_{\alpha} is the (time-independent) discrete Wigner function of the initial state, and OαW​(t)O^{W}_{\alpha}(t) is the Weyl symbol evolved in time. In practice one samples α\alpha from wαw_{\alpha} and propagates classical spin variables 𝐬i\mathbf{s}_{i} with the Hamiltonian HC​({𝐬})H_{C}(\{\mathbf{s}\}) obtained by replacing σ^iμ→siμ\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{\mu}\!\to s_{i}^{\mu}:

s˙iα={siα,HC}=2​∑β​γεα​β​γ​siγ​∂HC∂siβ.\dot{s}_{i}^{\alpha}=\{s_{i}^{\alpha},H_{C}\}=2\sum_{\beta\gamma}\varepsilon_{\alpha\beta\gamma}\,s_{i}^{\gamma}\,\frac{\partial H_{C}}{\partial s_{i}^{\beta}}. (29)

Averages over ntn_{t} samples yield statistical errors ∼nt−1/2\sim n_{t}^{-1/2}, where ntn_{t} is the number of samples, largely independent of NN.

TW is able to capture certain correlations over a finite time provided that the initial state can be sampled with classical trajectories. An important class of such initial states are factorizable spin states. TW has been used and verified to describe correlations in spin systems with short and long-range interactions [67]. The true advantage of TW is its modest computational cost in comparison to other more strongly correlated methods or advanced mean-field theories such as those based on FGS described in the previous paragraph. In the single-sample, no-fluctuation limit TW reduces to SMF.

Results:

Figure 20 summarizes the results from the mean-field and semiclassical methods introduced above. We compare the results for a (10×10)(10\times 10) square lattice only against MPS data in order to avoid clutter. The MPS data fulfilling the convergence criteria discussed in the main text are indicated by hollow circles. We compute the single-site magnetization ⟨σr0z⟩\langle\sigma^{z}_{r_{0}}\rangle in the top row and central site connected-correlation C⁡(δ1)C(\delta_{1}) in the bottom row for the regimes hx/J∈{0.5,2,3}h_{x}/J\in\{0.5,2,3\} in the respective columns of Figs.(a)-(f). For all mean-field and semiclassical methods we solve the equations of motion using a fourth order Runge-Kutta method at step size Δ​t=0.001\Delta t=0.001. For hx/J∈{0.5,3}h_{x}/J\in\{0.5,3\} we used nt=180000n_{t}=180000 and 200000200000 samples, while for hx/J=2.0h_{x}/J=2.0 we used nt=300000n_{t}=300000 and 400000400000 samples for the TW method (‘TW’). We use the PV-FGS for two different basis of the Ising Hamiltonian, i) the original basis where all interactions are described by σkz​σlz\sigma^{z}_{k}\sigma^{z}_{l}-interactions (‘FGS’) and ii) a rotated basis where the interactions are described by σkx​σlx\sigma^{x}_{k}\sigma^{x}_{l} (‘FGS XX’). In the ZZ and XX bases, the initial states are given by |00​…​0⟩\ket{00\dots 0} and 2−N/2(|0⟩+|1⟩)⊗N2^{-N/2}(\ket{0}+\ket{1})^{\otimes N}, respectively. Overall, we find the PV-FGS XX results outperform the results PV-FGS ZZ in all regimes. The spin-mean field solution (‘SMF’) fails to describe the qualitative behavior of MPS across all regimes. PV-FGS XX is able to capture the behavior of both observables in the low-field regime hx/J=0.5h_{x}/J=0.5, but fails to describe the high-field regime hx/J=3.0h_{x}/J=3.0. In contrast, the initial behavior of TW accurately captures the initial dynamics in the high-field regime, before converging to a classical equilibrium state. However, TW completely fails in describing the connected correlation functions in the low-field limit. All mean-field and semiclassical methods studied here fail to describe the dynamics of the considered observables at hx/J=2.0h_{x}/J=2.0 already after the first oscillation.
